claims.claim: MGE and POA-derived cortical interneurons express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST).
claims.source: MGE and POA-derived CINs express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST), while CGE-derived CINs express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin [but lack SST].
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: CGE-derived cortical interneurons express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin but lack SST.
claims.source: MGE and POA-derived CINs express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST), while CGE-derived CINs express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin [but lack SST].
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Hippocampal interneurons are generated by the same general progenitor pools as cortical interneurons and share similar molecular properties.
claims.source: HINs are generated by the same general progenitor pools and share similar molecular properties with CINs.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: There are no clear single markers known to define developing or mature hippocampal interneurons from cortical interneurons.
claims.source: However, so far there are no clear single markers that are known to define developing or mature HINs from CINs (Pelkey et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous literature (Pelkey et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Maf and Mafb function together in the MGE to control the timing and quantity of SST+ cortical interneurons that are generated.
claims.source: We have recently demonstrated that two Maf TFs, Maf (c-Maf) and Mafb, function together in the MGE to control the timing and quantity of SST+ CINs that are generated (Pai et al., 2019), schematically summarized in Schemes 1–3.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Loss of Mafb and Maf in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage leads to the overproduction of SST+ cortical interneurons at the expense of PV+ cortical interneurons.
claims.source: Loss of Mafb and Maf in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage (Maf cDKO) leads to the overproduction of SST+ CINs at the expense of PV+ CINs.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs have reduced cortical interneurons (~30%) at P0.
claims.source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs have increased hippocampal interneurons (~2 fold) at P0.
claims.source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs have a progressive loss of interneurons that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction.
claims.source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb alters postnatal cortical interneuron properties, including process morphogenesis, synaptogenesis, intrinsic electrophysiology and circuit excitability.
claims.source: Loss of Maf and Mafb also alters postnatal CIN properties, including process morphogenesis, synaptogenesis, intrinsic electrophysiology and circuit excitability (Pai et al., 2019; Schemes 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Adult Maf cDKOs have spontaneous non-motor epileptic activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, adult Maf cDKOs have spontaneous non-motor epileptic activity, likely associated with the interneuronopathy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EEG recording data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Single cell RNA-sequencing identified 24 different clusters from P0 WT and cDKO neocortices, including excitatory neurons, neural progenitors, microglia as well as MGE and CGE-derived interneurons.
claims.source: We identified 24 different clusters, including excitatory neurons, neural progenitors, microglia as well as MGE and CGE-derived INs, which were visualized by uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (Figure 1B and C; Becht et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: MGE-derived interneurons were in cluster 1, based on marker gene co-expression, including LIM homeobox 6 (Lhx6), Maf, Mafb and neurexophilin 1 (Nxph1).
claims.source: MGE-derived INs were in cluster 1, based on marker gene co-expression, including LIM homeobox 6 (Lhx6), Maf, Mafb and neurexophilin 1 (Nxph1) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Nxph1 is specifically expressed within the Nkx2.1-lineage.
claims.source: We performed fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm the specificity of Nxph1 expression within the Nkx2.1-lineage by co-labeling Nxph1 and Nkx2.1-Cre driven tdTomato (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: There were no obvious transcriptomic changes in neural progenitors, excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia and the CGE-derived interneuron population between WT and cDKO.
claims.source: There were no obvious transcriptomic changes in neural progenitors, excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia and the CGE-derived IN population between WT and cDKO (Figure 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1B and C showing no separation of WT and cDKO cells in non-MGE clusters.

claims.claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb in the Nkx2.1-Cre-lineage has no gross non-cell autonomous effects.
claims.source: This suggests no gross non-cell autonomous effects exerted by loss of Maf and Mafb in the Nkx2.1-Cre-lineage.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the lack of transcriptomic changes in non-MGE cell populations.

claims.claim: The MGE-derived interneuron population (cluster 1) showed clear differences between WT and cDKO.
claims.source: However, the MGE-derived IN population (cluster 1) showed clear differences between WT and cDKO (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1C showing separation of WT and cDKO cells in cluster 1.

claims.claim: Differential gene expression analysis in MGE-derived interneurons identified 81 differentially expressed genes, with 47 upregulated and 34 down-regulated in the Maf cDKO.
claims.source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Upregulated genes in Maf cDKO MGE-derived interneurons include Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y.
claims.source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Down-regulated genes in Maf cDKO MGE-derived interneurons include Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25.
claims.source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis showed that most dysregulated genes are involved in synapse formation, neurite projection and neuronal maturation.
claims.source: Gene ontology analysis, based upon cellular components, showed that most dysregulated genes are involved in synapse formation, neurite projection and neuronal maturation.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene in Maf cDKO MGE derived interneurons.
claims.source: Based on DEX analysis, Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene, while Sst was the most upregulated gene (Figure 1F–G, S7).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Sst was the most upregulated gene in Maf cDKO MGE derived interneurons.
claims.source: Based on DEX analysis, Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene, while Sst was the most upregulated gene (Figure 1F–G, S7).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: MEF2C expression was reduced in tdTomato+ cortical interneurons across all cortical layers in P2 cDKOs.
claims.source: To validate the Mef2c result, we used immunofluorescence labeling; MEF2C expression was reduced in the tdTomato+ CINs across all cortical layers in the P2 cDKOs (Figure 1F and L–N) (Bin 3, 4, 7: p<0.05; Bin 5, 6: p<0.01; Density: p<0.01; Welch's t test)
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1L-N with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: P2 cDKOs have increased Sst ISH signal and increased numbers of Sst+ cortical interneurons.
claims.source: To validate the Sst result, we used FISH; we found both increased Sst ISH signal and increased numbers of Sst+ CINs at P2 in cDKOs as before (Figure 1G and H–J) (Sst density: p=0.0001, Welch's t test) (Pai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1H-J with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: There was a > 3 fold increase in Sst and EdU double labeled cortical interneurons in P2 cDKO neocortices born at E15.5.
claims.source: There was a > 3 fold increase in Sst and EdU double labeled CINs in P2 cDKO neocortices (Figure 1K) (Sst-EdU density: p<0.0001; Welch's t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 1K with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs overproduce Sst+ cortical interneurons across development.
claims.source: Thus, Maf cDKOs overproduce Sst+ CINs across development.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the EdU labeling experiments showing increased Sst+ CINs at multiple developmental time points.

claims.claim: Prenatal loss of Mef2c reduces the number of PV+ cortical interneurons.
claims.source: Prenatal loss of Mef2c reduces the number of PV+ CINs (Mayer et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous literature (Mayer et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Maf and Mafb are genetically upstream of Mef2c.
claims.source: Given our finding that Mef2c expression is reduced in Maf cDKOs (Figure 1), it suggests that Maf and Mafb are genetically upstream of Mef2c.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the observation that Mef2c expression is reduced in Maf cDKOs.

claims.claim: Deficits in Mef2c potentially underlie the mechanisms causal to the PV+ cortical interneuron loss in the Maf cDKO.
claims.source: We thus hypothesized that deficits in Mef2c potentially underlie the mechanisms causal to the PV+ CIN loss in the Maf cDKO (this report; Pai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on the observation that Mef2c is reduced in cDKOs and that Mef2c loss reduces PV+ INs.

claims.claim: Maf cDKO MGE cells have reduced PV+ cortical interneurons in transplantation assays.
claims.source: The analysis confirmed the preferential loss of PV+ CINs in the cDKOs (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Mef2c transfection rescued the PV+ cortical interneuron deficit in Maf cDKO MGE cells.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that Mef2c transfection rescued this phenotype, and corrected the SST/PV ratio (Figure 2B and K) (PV population: WT vs. cDKO p<0.0001; cDKO vs. cDKO+Mef2c p<0.0001; Chi-square test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2B and K with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression, which in turn promotes the PV+ interneuron fate.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression, which in turn promotes the PV+ IN fate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Model).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that Mef2c can restore PV+ IN production in cDKOs.

claims.claim: Within MGE-derived interneurons, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ interneurons.
claims.source: We hypothesize that within MGE-derived INs, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ INs, in part since Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ INs remain SST+ (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing data.

claims.claim: Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ interneurons remain SST+.
claims.source: We hypothesize that within MGE-derived INs, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ INs, in part since Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ INs remain SST+ (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Arl4d, Elmo1, Igfbp4, Mef2c, Sp9 and Tcf12 are enriched in the Sst- MGE-derived interneuron population.
claims.source: We identified a group of genes that are enriched in the Sst- population, by comparing the IN marker expression between the two groups (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). From these, we selected six genes, ADP ribosylation factor like GTPase 4D (Arl4d), engulfment and cell motility protein 1 (Elmo1), insulin like growth factor binding protein 4 (Igfbp4), Mef2c, Sp9 and transcription factor 12 (Tcf12), with high-to-moderate expression to evaluate their RNA expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Mef2c is a very specific Sst- population marker, especially in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Our results suggested that Mef2c is a very specific Sst- population marker, especially in the hippocampus (Cortex: p<0.05; Hippocampus: p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Elmo1, Igfbp4, and Sp9 are good markers for Sst- MGE-derived interneurons in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Likewise, Elmo1, Igfbp4, and Sp9 appear to be good markers for Sst- MGE-derived INs in the hippocampus (Elmo1: p<0.001; Igfbp4: p<0.05; Tcf12: p<0.01; unpaired test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: This is the first study to identify genes that are almost exclusively expressed in Sst- MGE-derived immature hippocampal interneurons.
claims.source: This likely is the first study to identify genes, such as Mef2c, that are almost exclusively expressed in Sst- MGE-derived immature HINs.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and represents a novel finding of the study.

claims.claim: Reduced expression of Mef2c and Snap25 impedes neurite morphogenesis.
claims.source: Reduced expression of Mef2c and Snap25 was shown to impede neurite morphogenesis (Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature (Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs have a neurite outgrowth defect in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: Since Maf cDKOs have a neurite outgrowth defect in vitro and in vivo (Pai et al., 2019, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we examined whether the decreased expression of Mef2c and Snap25 in the cDKOs underlies their neurite outgrowth defect (Pai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019) and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: cDKO cortical interneurons had decreased numbers of neurites.
claims.source: As before, cDKO CINs had decreased numbers of neurites; Gfp transfection did not alter this phenotype (Figure 4B, C and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Transfection of cDKO with Maf, Mef2c or Snap25 rescued neurite numbers to levels comparable to WT.
claims.source: Second, transfection of cDKO with Maf, Mef2c or Snap25 rescued neurite numbers, and the increased neurite numbers were comparable to WT (Figure 4B, D–F and H–I).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Reduced Mef2c and Snap25 expression are downstream of Maf and Mafb in regulating neurite complexity in neonatal cortical interneurons.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that reduced Mef2c and Snap25 expression are downstream of Maf and Mafb in regulating neurite complexity in neonatal CINs.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Sst-IRES-Cre generated Maf cDKO interneurons have neurite defects similar to those found using Nkx2.1-Cre.
claims.source: We found that the Sst-IRES-Cre generated Maf cDKO had neurite defects similar to those found using Nkx2.1-Cre.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Maf function in neurite outgrowth is required post-mitotically.
claims.source: Thus, Maf function in neurite outgrowth is also required post-mitotically.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the Sst-IRES-Cre experiments showing neurite defects when Maf is deleted post-mitotically.

claims.claim: Postnatal deletion of Maf and Mafb in cortical interneurons (cDKOPOST) resulted in reduced neurite complexity.
claims.source: At DIV14, we performed Sholl analysis, which revealed that cDKOPOST INs had reduced neurite complexity, providing evidence that Maf and Mafb regulate IN morphology postnatally.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Maf and Mafb regulate interneuron morphology postnatally.
claims.source: At DIV14, we performed Sholl analysis, which revealed that cDKOPOST INs had reduced neurite complexity, providing evidence that Maf and Mafb regulate IN morphology postnatally.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the postnatal deletion experiments.

claims.claim: Maf, Mef2c and Snap25 each rescued the neurite outgrowth defect in postnatal Maf cDKO interneurons.
claims.source: Maf, Mef2c and Snap25 each rescued the neurite outgrowth defect (Figure 4K–R).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4K-R.

claims.claim: Maf and Mafb likely promote cortical interneuron neurite morphogenesis at postnatal stages through Mef2c and Snap25.
claims.source: Thus, Maf and Mafb likely promote CIN neurite morphogenesis at postnatal stages through Mef2c and Snap25.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the postnatal rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Prepronociceptin (Pnoc) was an upregulated gene in the Maf cDKO.
claims.source: The DEX analysis revealed that prepronociceptin (Pnoc) was an upregulated gene in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Pnoc is a marker of O-LM interneurons, a subtype that is mainly Sst+.
claims.source: A recent study focusing on adult CA1 HIN profiling suggested Pnoc is a marker of O-LM INs, a subtype that is mainly Sst+ (Harris et al., 2018; Asgarian et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature (Harris et al., 2018; Asgarian et al., 2019).

claims.claim: In P2 WTs, Pnoc+ cells were largely restricted to the hippocampus.
claims.source: In P2 WTs, Pnoc+ cells were largely restricted to the hippocampus (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: ~40% of the Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons are tdTomato+ (Nkx2.1-Cre lineage).
claims.source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Very few Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons are Htr3a+ (CGE marker).
claims.source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The MGE/POA is the main origin of Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons.
claims.source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the observation that many Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+ (MGE/POA lineage) and few are Htr3a+ (CGE lineage).

claims.claim: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex, highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus.
claims.source: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex (highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus), as well as increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus, consistent with an increased density of HINs (Figure 5A–L) (WT vs cDKO: Neocortex p<0.01; dorsomedial Neocortex p<0.0001; Hippocampus p<0.01; t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5A-L with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Maf cDKO has increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus.
claims.source: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex (highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus), as well as increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus, consistent with an increased density of HINs (Figure 5A–L) (WT vs cDKO: Neocortex p<0.01; dorsomedial Neocortex p<0.0001; Hippocampus p<0.01; t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5A-L with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Sst FISH and tdTomato+ interneuron quantifications both suggested increased hippocampal interneuron density in the Maf cDKO.
claims.source: Indeed, Sst FISH and tdTomato+ IN quantifications both suggested increased HIN density in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH and quantification data shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb leads to increased production of hippocampal interneurons, which are mainly Sst+ and/or Pnoc+.
claims.source: Together, these data provide evidence that loss of Maf and Mafb leads to increased production of HINs, which are mainly Sst+ and/or Pnoc+.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the FISH data showing increased Sst+ and Pnoc+ HINs in cDKOs.

claims.claim: Lhx6+ cortical interneuron density was decreased in Maf cDKOs at P2.
claims.source: Lhx6+ CIN density was decreased in Maf cDKOs as previously reported (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: There was an increased density of Lhx6+ hippocampal interneurons across all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO at P2.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, there was an increased density of Lhx6+ HINs across all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO (p<0.05; Welch's t test) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: There was an increased density of Sst+ hippocampal interneurons in all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO at P2.
claims.source: Furthermore, there was an increased density of Sst+ HINs cell density in all hippocampal regions (CA1:~1.5 fold; p<0.001, CA3 and DG:~2 fold; p<0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: At E12.5, Maf cDKOs showed ~2 fold increase in hippocampal interneuron generation.
claims.source: At E12.5 (early-born; Lhx6+;BrdU+), we observed ~2 fold increase in HIN generation in the Maf cDKO (p<0.01; t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The increase in hippocampal interneuron generation at E12.5 was similar across all hippocampal subregions in Maf cDKOs.
claims.source: The increase was similar across all hippocampal subregions (Figure 6D, E, H and I) (CA1: p=0.02; CA3: p<0.001; DG: p<0.01; t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Maf cDKOs had a trend toward decreased cortical interneuron generation at E12.5.
claims.source: In contrast, Maf cDKOs had a trend toward decreased CIN generation at E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At E15.5, Maf cDKOs showed ~2.5 fold increase in hippocampal interneuron production.
claims.source: At E15.5 (late-born; Lhx6+;EdU+), we observed ~2.5 fold increase in HIN production (p<0.0001; t test).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

results.result: Adult Maf cDKO mice exhibit spontaneous non-motor epileptic activity characterized by spike-and-wave discharges similar to absence-type epilepsy. The authors propose this epileptic phenotype is multifaceted, involving overall reductions in MGE-derived interneurons and dysregulation of genes including Mef2c, Snap25, and Npy.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C131 are directly supported by EEG recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrating spike-and-wave discharges in cDKO mice. Claims C132-C134 provide mechanistic context through citations to prior work and are consistent with the observed interneuronopathy. The statistical comparison (C23) shows significant differences between WT and cDKO.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing of P0 WT and cDKO neocortices identified 24 clusters including MGE-derived interneurons (cluster 1). Differential expression analysis revealed 81 dysregulated genes in MGE interneurons, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc, Npy) and 34 downregulated (including Maf, Mafb, Mef2c, Cxcr4, Snap25). No transcriptomic changes were observed in non-MGE cell types, suggesting cell-autonomous effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C33 are well-supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures. UMAP visualization (C24, C29) clearly shows cluster separation for MGE interneurons but not other cell types (C27). Differential expression analysis (C30-C32) is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 5. Validation by FISH and immunofluorescence for key genes (C36-C37) strengthens these findings. Gene ontology analysis (C33) provides functional context.

results.result: Mef2c was the third most downregulated gene while Sst was the most upregulated gene in Maf cDKO MGE interneurons. Validation by immunofluorescence confirmed reduced MEF2C expression across cortical layers in P2 cDKOs, and FISH confirmed increased Sst+ cortical interneurons. Birth-dating experiments showed >3-fold increase in Sst+ interneurons born at E15.5, indicating overproduction across development.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are strongly supported by converging evidence from scRNA-seq (C34-C35), immunofluorescence (C36), FISH (C37), and EdU birth-dating (C38). Statistical analyses are provided for all quantifications with appropriate p-values. The conclusion of persistent overproduction (C39) is a reasonable inference from the temporal data showing increased Sst+ INs at multiple developmental stages.

results.result: Maf and Mafb are genetically upstream of Mef2c and promote its expression to drive PV+ interneuron fate specification. MGE transplantation assays confirmed reduced PV+ interneurons in cDKO cells, and Mef2c transfection rescued this deficit, correcting the SST/PV ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are directly supported by transplantation data in Figure 2 with appropriate statistical analysis (Chi-square test, p<0.0001). The genetic relationship (C41) is a reasonable inference from the observation that Mef2c is reduced in cDKOs. Claim C40 is supported by citation to prior work. The rescue experiment (C44) provides strong functional evidence for the proposed pathway (C45). However, C42 is labeled as speculation/hypothesis, which is appropriate.

results.result: The authors identified candidate markers of immature PV+ interneurons by comparing Sst+ and Sst- MGE-derived interneurons. Mef2c, Elmo1, Igfbp4, and Sp9 are enriched in Sst- populations, particularly in the hippocampus. This represents the first identification of genes almost exclusively expressed in Sst- MGE-derived immature hippocampal interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 3A) and validated by RNAscope with statistical comparisons (Figure 3). The hypothesis that Sst- cells represent future PV+ interneurons (C46) is reasonable based on lineage tracing data (C47, cited from prior work). The specificity of markers, particularly Mef2c in hippocampus (C49, p<0.0001), is well-documented. Claim C51 regarding novelty is appropriately qualified as "likely" the first such study.

results.result: Reduced Mef2c and Snap25 expression underlie neurite outgrowth defects in Maf cDKO interneurons. Primary culture experiments showed that transfection of Maf, Mef2c, or Snap25 each rescued neurite complexity defects in cDKO interneurons to WT levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by Sholl analysis data in Figure 4 showing reduced neurite complexity in cDKO and rescue by all three genes. Claim C52 is supported by citations to prior literature. The conclusion (C56) that Mef2c and Snap25 are downstream of Maf/Mafb is a reasonable inference from the rescue experiments, though alternative explanations (e.g., parallel pathways) are not fully excluded. Sample sizes appear adequate (N=3-4 per group, 15-20 neurons analyzed).

results.result: Maf and Mafb have post-mitotic functions in regulating interneuron morphology. Deletion using Sst-IRES-Cre (post-mitotic) or postnatal deletion in culture both resulted in neurite outgrowth defects. Maf, Mef2c, and Snap25 each rescued neurite defects in postnatal cDKO interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C59 are supported by Sholl analysis data from Sst-IRES-Cre experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and postnatal deletion experiments (Figure 4). The rescue experiments (C61) are documented in Figure 4K-R. The inference of post-mitotic function (C58, C60) is well-supported by the experimental design, which specifically tests function after cell cycle exit. The conclusion (C62) is appropriately qualified as "likely" given the rescue data.

results.result: Prepronociceptin (Pnoc) is identified as a hippocampal interneuron-specific marker. In P2 WTs, Pnoc+ cells are largely restricted to hippocampus, with ~40% being tdTomato+ (MGE/POA lineage) and few being Htr3a+ (CGE lineage). Maf cDKOs show ectopic Pnoc expression in neocortex and increased Pnoc+ cells in hippocampus, consistent with increased hippocampal interneuron density.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 are well-supported by FISH data in Figure 5 with appropriate statistical analyses (t-tests with p<0.01 to p<0.0001). The spatial restriction of Pnoc to hippocampus in WTs (C65) is clearly shown in Figure 5G. Lineage analysis (C66-C67) provides evidence for MGE/POA origin. The increased Pnoc expression in cDKO (C69-C70) is quantified across regions. The conclusion (C72) is a reasonable inference supported by converging evidence from Pnoc, Sst, and tdTomato quantifications.

results.result: Maf and Mafb repress hippocampal interneuron generation. Birth-dating experiments showed ~2-fold increase in hippocampal interneuron generation at E12.5 and ~2.5-fold increase at E15.5 in cDKOs, across all hippocampal subregions. In contrast, cortical interneuron generation showed a trend toward decrease at E12.5. The MGE normally generates hippocampal/cortical interneurons in a 1:2 ratio, but cDKOs overproduce hippocampal interneurons, especially at E12.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C82 are supported by comprehensive birth-dating experiments using BrdU (E12.5) and EdU (E15.5) with Lhx6 FISH (Figure 6). Statistical analyses are provided for all quantifications (t-tests with p<0.01 to p<0.0001). The regional specificity (C77, C80) is documented across CA1, CA3, and DG. The conclusion (C83) that hippocampal interneuron overproduction occurs "at the expense" of cortical interneurons is appropriately qualified as a hypothesis ("perhaps") given the trend data for cortical interneurons (C78).

results.result: Cxcr4 expression is reduced in Maf cDKO MGE interneurons, starting as early as E15.5. FISH at P2 showed clear reduction especially in hippocampus. While this provides a potential mechanism for premature interneuron entrance into the cortical plate, reduced Cxcr4 alone probably does not explain increased hippocampal interneurons, as Cxcr4 null mice do not show this phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and validated by FISH (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) with statistical analyses (p=0.0159 for hippocampus, p<0.0001 for neocortex). The inference regarding migration defects (C116) is reasonable given prior work cited. The conclusion (C118) that Cxcr4 reduction alone is insufficient is appropriately cautious and supported by comparison to Cxcr4 null mice (C117, cited from prior work).

results.result: Nrp1 is upregulated in Maf cDKO, particularly in hippocampus. While Nrp1 overexpression alone is not sufficient to promote increased hippocampal/cortical interneuron ratio, the authors propose that interactions between NRP1 and CXCR4 may guide interneuron migration to hippocampus, based on analogies to other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by differential expression analysis and FISH data (Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 7). Claims C121-C129 provide relevant background from prior literature. However, the key mechanistic claim (C130) is speculative and not directly tested. The negative result from Nrp1 overexpression experiments (C123, mentioned in discussion but data not shown) weakens the proposed mechanism. The analogy to other systems (breast cancer, visual system) may not be directly applicable to interneuron development.

results.result: The authors propose a transcriptional pathway where Maf/Mafb drive Mef2c expression to promote PV+ interneuron production prenatally and interneuron morphological maturation postnatally. This pathway may operate in conjunction with signaling hubs such as MTOR/MAPK/RYK.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 provide established background on Mef2c from prior literature. Claims C87, C89, C96 are directly supported by rescue experiments (Figures 2 and 4). Claims C90-C91 are supported by birth-dating data. The proposed pathway (C92) is a reasonable synthesis of the experimental findings, though direct evidence of transcriptional regulation (e.g., ChIP-seq, promoter analysis) is not provided. The speculation about signaling pathways (C93) is appropriately qualified and supported by citations. Claims C95 and C97 regarding persistent postnatal function are well-supported by the postnatal deletion experiments.

results.result: Snap25 is part of the SNARE complex regulating vesicle fusion and neurite branching. Snap25 expression is decreased in Maf cDKO interneurons, and expressing Snap25 rescued neurite outgrowth defects in both prenatal and postnatal cDKO interneurons. The authors propose that Snap25 and Mef2c may regulate each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 provide established background supported by citations. Claim C100 is supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). Claim C101 is directly supported by rescue experiments in Figure 4. The conclusion (C102) that Maf/Mafb-driven expression of Snap25 is critical is well-supported by the rescue data. However, the speculation about mutual regulation between Snap25 and Mef2c (C103) is not directly tested and remains hypothetical.

results.result: Maf and Mafb are key regulators of disease genes responsible for balanced MGE SST/PV interneuron production (Mef2c), interneuron morphological maturation (Mef2c, Snap25), and balanced cortical/hippocampal interneuron production (Cxcr4, Nrp1). The authors report that ~22% of Nkx2.1-Cre lineage cortical interneurons are Sp9+ at P2, with ~60% of PV candidate hippocampal interneurons being Sp9+.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is a reasonable summary of the study's findings, synthesizing the various experimental results. Claims C136-C138 regarding Sp9 expression are supported by RNAscope quantification data mentioned in the discussion. The novelty claim (C137) is appropriately stated. The acknowledgment that 22% may be an underestimate (C138) shows appropriate scientific caution. However, the Sp9 data appears to be primarily in the discussion without detailed presentation in main figures.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior work: Maf and Mafb have compensatory roles in repressing SST+ interneuron production in MGE secondary progenitors. Maf/Mafb conditional deletion decreases survival and changes physiological properties of MGE-derived cortical interneurons. Loss of Maf/Mafb leads to overproduction of SST+ interneurons at expense of PV+ interneurons, with progressive interneuron loss reaching ~70% by adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C17-C22 are all explicitly stated as being from prior work (Pai et al., 2019) and are appropriately cited throughout. These claims provide essential context for the current study. While not new findings in this manuscript, they are accurately represented and properly attributed. The evidence type is correctly labeled as CITATION and DATA from prior work.

results.result: Background claims on interneuron biology: Interneuron pathologies are hypothesized to underlie symptoms of autism, epilepsy, and schizophrenia through disrupted circuit inhibition. Cortical interneurons are generated in MGE, CGE, and POA, with distinct molecular markers. Hippocampal interneurons share similar properties with cortical interneurons but lack clear distinguishing markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 represent established knowledge in the field, appropriately cited to prior literature (Lim et al., 2018; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011; Gelman et al., 2011; Pelkey et al., 2017). These claims provide necessary background context and are accurately represented. The gap in knowledge regarding hippocampal interneuron markers (C16) sets up one of the study's contributions.

results.result: Discussion claims on Pnoc as hippocampal interneuron marker: The molecular program distinguishing cortical from hippocampal interneurons remains largely unknown. The authors identify Pnoc as a unique marker distinguishing hippocampal from cortical interneurons, with expression widely and robustly in hippocampal but not cortical interneurons. Loss of Maf/Mafb leads to increased Pnoc expression and disproportionate hippocampal interneurons, suggesting Maf/Mafb control cortical/hippocampal interneuron regional fate determination.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C112 synthesize the Pnoc findings in the discussion. The gap in knowledge (C104) is appropriately stated. The identification of Pnoc as a marker (C105, C108) is well-supported by FISH data in Figure 5. Prior work on Pnoc (C106-C107) is appropriately cited. The increased expression in cDKO (C109) is supported by quantification. The conclusions about Maf/Mafb controlling regional fate (C110-C112) are reasonable inferences from the data, representing a novel finding of the study.
